# Overview of this FAQ and how to get help

This is a list of some frequently asked questions (FAQ) on the GSVA package,
with answers and links to the relevant documentation and resources. If you have
any other question that you would like to see included in this FAQ, please
open an [issue](https://github.com/rcastelo/GSVA/issues) in the GSVA GitHub
repo. Aside from this FAQ and opening a GitHub issue, you can also get help on
the GSVA package by:

1. Using the help system in R, e.g. `?gsva` or `help(gsva)`, and reading the
   package vignettes, which can be accessed from your own software installation
   with `browseVignettes("GSVA")`, or through the Bioconductor landing page for
   the GSVA package at https://bioconductor.org/packages/GSVA.

2. Posting your question on the
   [Bioconductor support site](https://support.bioconductor.org), after reading
   the [Bioconductor posting guide](https://bioconductor.org/help/support/posting-guide).

# How do I cite GSVA?

If you use the GSVA package in your research, please cite the GSVA publication
[@haenzelmann2013gsva]. Additionally, if you use any of the following methods
implemented in the GSVA package, please cite the corresponding publications:

  * _ssGSEA_ [@barbie_systematic_2009].

  * _Z-score_ [@lee_inferring_2008].

  * _PLAGE_ [@tomfohr_pathway_2005].

# Common error messages and how to fix them

## There is no package called 'GSVA'

If you encounter the error:

```{sh, eval=FALSE}
Error in library(GSVA) : there is no package called 'GSVA'
```
This is because the GSVA package is not installed. You can install it with:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("GSVA")
```

## Could not find function "gsva"

If you encounter the error:

```{sh, eval=FALSE}
Error in gsva() : could not find function "gsva"
```
This is because the GSVA package is not loaded. You can load it with:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(GSVA)
```

## Unable to find an inherited method for function ‘gsva’ for signature

If you encounter one of the following two errors, the first one given by some
versions of GSVA:

```{sh, eval=FALSE}
Error in gsva(): Calling gsva(expr=., gset.idx.list=., method=., ...) is defunct

[... or ...]

Error: unable to find an inherited method for function ‘gsva’ for signature ‘param = "matrix"’
```
where the last part could also be `param = "SummarizedExperiment"`,
`param = "SingleCellExperiment"`, `param = "SpatialExperiment"`, etc., this is
because you are providing a wrong first argument in the call to `gsva()`. In
versions < 1.50 (up to October 2023, Bioconductor release 3.17), this first
argument was the object containing the input expression data. However, starting
with version 1.50 (October 2023, Bioconductor release 3.18), the first argument
should be an object of class `GsvaMethodParam` built with a constructor function
according to the method you want to use, i.e., `gsvaParam()`, `ssgseaParam()`,
`zscoreParam()`, `plageParam()` or `avgParam()`, as in:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
gsva(gsvaParam(expr, gsets))
```
See the first [GSVA package vignette](https://bioconductor.org/packages/GSVA)
for more details and examples.

## No identifiers in the gene sets could be matched to the identifiers in the expression data

If you encounter the error:

```{sh, eval=FALSE}
No identifiers in the gene sets could be matched to the identifiers in the expression data
```
It means that none of the identifiers in your gene sets could be matched to the
identifiers in your expression data. This is usually because the identifiers in
your gene sets are of a different type than the identifiers in your expression
data, and both input expression and gene sets lack the necessary metadata to
map one type onto the other. For example, your gene sets may contain gene
symbols, while your expression data may contain Ensembl gene IDs. Other common
causes are Ensembl identifiers with a version suffix (e.g., `ENSG00000141510.17`
instead of `ENSG00000141510`), and gene sets of one organism used with data from
another one (e.g., human symbols such as `TP53` with mouse data, where the
symbol is `Trp53`).

The simplest way to provide the missing metadata on the expression data is the
`annotation` argument of the parameter constructor function, e.g.:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(GSEABase)

gsva(gsvaParam(expr, gsets, annotation=xxxxIdentifier("org.Xx.eg.db")))
```
where `xxxxIdentifier` is the appropriate function for the type of identifiers
in your expression data, e.g., `ENSEMBLIdentifier()`, `EntrezIdentifier()`,
etc. Note that you should load the package
[GSEABase](https://bioconductor.org/packages/GSEABase) to use these functions,
and you may obtain help about them by typing `help(GeneIdentifierType)`. Here
also `org.Xx.eg.db` is the appropriate organism-level annotation package for
your expression data, e.g., `org.Hs.eg.db` for human, `org.Mm.eg.db` for mouse,
etc. Please check the
[Bioconductor annotation packages](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/BiocViews.html#___AnnotationData)
for the available organism-level annotation packages. You can check whether
this metadata is present in your input expression data with
`gsvaAnnotation(expr)`, which returns `NULL` when it is missing, and you can
also add it to the expression data with the following instruction:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
gsvaAnnotation(expr) <- xxxxIdentifier("org.Xx.eg.db")
```

Gene sets read with `readGMT()` already have this metadata, which is guessed
from their identifiers. When `gsets` is a `list` object,
`gsvaAnnotation(gsets)` returns `NULL`, and you can add the metadata in the
same way as for the input expression data.

# Input data and scores

## How should the input expression data be pre-processed before running GSVA?

Our recommendation is to pre-process the input expression data in the same way
as you would do for a differential expression analysis, i.e., removing lowly
expressed genes and normalizing the columns of expression data to reduce
technical biases, such as differences in sequencing depth and RNA composition.
GSVA does not read normalization factors or offsets produced by some
normalization pipelines and associated with raw integer counts, so it is
necessary to use those factors or offsets to transform the input raw integer
counts into normalized continuous units of expression, such as log2 CPM, or
log2 TPM.

## Do the scores of a column depend on the other columns of the input data?

Yes, for the GSVA, Z-score and PLAGE methods, which normalize or decompose the
expression of each gene across all the columns of the input data. ssGSEA scores
depend on the other columns only through `normalize=TRUE`, the default, which
divides the scores by their range over the whole input data. Therefore, adding
or removing columns may change that normalizing range, which in turn may change
the resulting ssGSEA scores. If you do not want ssGSEA scores to be affected by
other columns use `ssgseaParam(..., normalize=FALSE)`. Note that this does not
imply that ssGSEA scores from disparate columns or datasets are directly
comparable.

## Why are some of my gene sets missing from the output?

Gene sets are first mapped to the rows of the input expression data, and those
genes in gene sets that are absent from the expression data, are removed from
each gene set. Then, gene sets with fewer than `minSize` or more than `maxSize`
genes are discarded. The gene sets actually used can be obtained by calling
`geneSets()` on the parameter object or on the output of `gsva()`.

## Why do scores differ from those of previous versions of the GSVA package?

The GSVA package includes _regression_ tests that are routinely run in the
Bioconductor [build system](https://bioconductor.org/checkResults) to detect
unintended changes in the scores with respect to previous versions of the
package, caused by, e.g., bugs or new features. So, in principle, given the
same input, scores should not differ with respect to previous versions of the
package. However, this can still happen in the following cases:

1. With any method, when one or more input gene sets contain duplicated gene
   identifiers. Such duplicates are uncommon in the input gene sets, but they
   can be introduced when mapping their identifiers to a different type, e.g.,
   when two gene symbols map to the same Ensembl gene identifier. Previous
   versions of the GSVA package did not detect them and included them in the
   calculations, biasing the scores. The current version removes them before
   the calculations.
2. With the GSVA method on single-cell or spatially resolved transcriptomics
   data, because zero values are now handled in a way that makes GSVA scores
   stable. In this type of data, the default row-normalization method has also
   changed to a more performant one (CLR). You can switch back to the previous
   method with the parameter `rowNorm` of `gsvaParam()`. Please consult
   `help(gsvaParam)` and the vignette on using GSVA with single-cell data.
3. With the GSVA method on input data with missing values, because random walks
   now run only over the non-missing genes of each column.
4. With the PLAGE method, whose sign, instead of being the arbitrary default of
   the singular value decomposition, is now set so that scores correlate
   positively with the mean expression of the gene set.
5. With GPU acceleration when calculating GSVA scores, because calculations are
   performed in single precision; please consult the vignette on using GSVA
   with GPU hardware.

# GSVA scores

## How do I interpret GSVA scores and fold changes between them?

GSVA first normalizes the expression of each gene across the columns of the
input data, so that each value reflects how high is the expression of that gene
in that column, relative to the other columns. A positive GSVA score for a
given gene set in a given column means that the genes of that gene set tend to
be more highly expressed in that column, relative to the other columns, than
the genes outside the gene set. A negative score means the opposite, and a
score close to zero means that the genes of the gene set show no such tendency.

Because of how GSVA scores are derived, the magnitude of a fold change or
difference in means between two groups of columns for a given gene set is
difficult to interpret, but you can interpret the direction (over-expression
or under-expression of that gene set or pathway). GSVA does not provide
p-values on any hypothesis test about the magnitude of the score, but you can
test with linear models whether a coefficient derived from GSVA scores is
significantly different from zero; see the subsection on differential expression
at pathway level of the first
[GSVA vignette](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/GSVA/inst/doc/GSVA.html#72_Differential_expression_at_pathway_level)
and the GSVA publication [@haenzelmann2013gsva] for further details.

## Why are some of the GSVA scores negative?

A GSVA score for a given gene set in a given column is negative when the genes
in that gene set are, relative to the other columns, less expressed in that
column than the genes outside that gene set. The function `gsvaEnrichment()`
produces an enrichment plot that helps to understand how a GSVA score was
calculated. Please also consult the GSVA publication [@haenzelmann2013gsva] for
more details on how the GSVA scores are calculated.

# ssGSEA scores

## Do the ssGSEA scores of GSVA differ from those of the Broad Institute implementation?

The implementation of ssGSEA in the GSVA package is based on the original
publication by Barbie et al. [@barbie_systematic_2009], and in principle the
resulting enrichment scores should be nearly identical to the scores obtained
with the first implementation by the authors of that publication, at the Broad
Institute, available at https://github.com/GSEA-MSigDB/ssGSEA-gpmodule, and as
the _ssGSEAProjection module_ in the
[GenePattern](https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/ssGSEAProjection/4)
software, provided that parameters such as the weight exponent (`alpha`) and
the normalization of the scores (`normalize`) match. There have been subsequent
versions of the ssGSEA algorithm by the Broad Institute,
[ssGSEA 2.0](https://github.com/broadinstitute/ssGSEA2.0) and
[ssGSEA 3.0](https://github.com/broadinstitute/ssGSEA3.0), which are not
implemented in the GSVA package.

# Large input expression datasets

## Can I run GSVA on a large input expression dataset that does not fit into main memory?

Yes, as long as it is stored on disk, e.g., in an HDF5 file, and given to GSVA
as a `DelayedArray` object, such as an `HDF5Array` object. If the dataset is
sparse, such as those produced by single-cell and spatially resolved
transcriptomics, substantial performance gains can be obtained when the file
only stores nonzero values as a compressed sparse column (CSC) matrix (e.g.,
[10x Genomics HDF5](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/cell-ranger-arc/latest/analysis/outputs/outputs-h5-matrices)).
With default parameters, GSVA will use 90% of the main memory of the computer
or, if smaller, of the memory limit of the job in a computer cluster. Memory
consumption can be controlled with the parameter `maxmem` in the calls to
`gsva()`, `gsvaRowNorm()`, `gsvaColRanks()` and `gsvaColScores()`,and whether
the calculations are performed on disk with the parameter `ondisk` in the
calls to `gsvaParam()`, `ssgseaParam()`, `zscoreParam()`, `plageParam()` and
`avgParam()`. Please consult the help pages of those functions for more details
on those parameters.

## Can I run GSVA calculations in parallel in my computer?

Yes, using the `BPPARAM` parameter in the calls to `gsva()`, `gsvaRowNorm()`,
`gsvaColRanks()` and `gsvaColScores()`, e.g.,
`gsva(param, BPPARAM=MulticoreParam(workers=4))`; please consult the details on
that parameter in the manual pages of those functions.

## Can I run GSVA calculations in parallel in a high-performance computing cluster?

Yes, using the functions `gsvaMap()` and `gsvaReduce()`; please consult the
package vignette entitled
[Using GSVA on GPUs, HPC clusters and the cloud](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/GSVA/inst/doc/GSVA_GPU_HPC_cloud.html).

# Interoperability with other software ecosystems

## Seurat objects

You can convert a Seurat object into a `SingleCellExperiment` object with the
function `as.SingleCellExperiment()` from the CRAN package
[Seurat](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=Seurat), and then use that object
as input to the `gsva()` function.

## scverse AnnData objects

You can read an AnnData `.h5ad` file into a `SingleCellExperiment` object with
the function `readH5AD()` from the Bioconductor package
[zellkonverter](https://bioconductor.org/packages/zellkonverter), or with the
function `read_h5ad()` from the Bioconductor package
[anndataR](https://bioconductor.org/packages/anndataR), and then use that object
as input to the `*Param()` parameter constructor functions. Please consult the
documentation of those packages for more details on how to use them.
